newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul moves to stop street collections for N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: Seoul moves to stop street collections for N.Korea.

text.p: South Korea said on Friday it would enforce a law banning street collections for starving North Koreans after a rash of fund raising by a variety of groups eager to ease the plight of their Northern neighbours.
Analysts say the move shows government fears that Pyongyang could be using the frenzy of cash collections for political gains.
The government said it would restrict fund raising after an umbrella organisation for several militant groups on Thursday launched a campaign to collect money to feed North Koreans.

The umbrella group, which calls itself the Love for Our Compatriots Coalition, includes a radical nationwide student organisation and the 500,000-member union that led last winter's nationwide labour strikes.

"The National Unification Ministry's position is that fund raising within an organisation is alright, but raising money on the streets is illegal," a ministry spokesman who declined to be identified told Reuters.

Political analysts said the fund-raising frenzy is interfering with the government's efforts to use food to lure Pyongyang to four-way peace talks proposed last April by Seoul and Washington. China would also participate.
The United States and South Korea are expecting a response by North Korea to a meeting set for next week in New York.
Rhee Sang-woo, a Sogang University political professor and a North Korean specialist, said the aid drives by Pyongyang sympathisers worry the government.
"They are afraid North Korea will use the movement for political gains," Rhee said.
"The government is an acrobat trying to bow to public sentiment to send aid while it knows North Korea is conducting expensive large military exercises."

South Korea has contributed $6 million and has said it will give more to an aid package being put together by the U.N.'s World Food Programme. Seoul also said it would allow business and civilian groups to donate rice to Pyongyang.

But the National Unification Minister Kwon O-kie said last Friday the North could relieve its food shortage "if it only saved one or two percent" from the "billions of dollars spent on the military and on propaganda".

An official in the ministry's aid division who asked not to be identified said in an interview: "The law can be applied flexibly. If the campaign doesn't cause social unrest and the purpose is only to help feed North Koreans, then there is no reason to cause friction by enforcing the law."
Kim Sung-yeoun at Korea Sharing Movement, comprising religious and civic groups, said it is planning to set up street stalls for its drive. Its goal is to raise 17 billion won ($19 million).
"I don't think we will have any problems. The government has been cooperative," said Kim.
The Korea Sharing Movement was allowed to raise funds in the street in March.
The more militant Compatriots Coalition was less positive about being permitted to collect donations on the street.
"We're all trying to help our brethren North Koreans. Why should leftist or rightist ideology be an issue?" said Kim Hyun-bae, an organisation leader. "There seem to be two measuring sticks."
"We will start our fund raising on Monday regardless of the law."
